title: Sitaula urges Shekhar Koirala and Purna Bahadur Khadka to end neutrality in Nepali Congress dispute - OnlineKhabar English News
description: Sitaula urges Shekhar Koirala and Purna Bahadur Khadka to end neutrality in Nepali Congress dispute  OnlineKhabar English News
publisher.title: OnlineKhabar English News
full_article:
Biratnagar, November 17

Nepali Congress former general secretary Krishna Prasad Sitaula has urged party leaders who have remained neutral in the ongoing internal dispute to make their positions clear.

Addressing the Morang district convention organised by supporters of former party president Sher Bahadur Deuba on Tuesday, Sitaula said remaining neutral would not help resolve disputes within a party or a family. He said the leaders who had stayed neutral needed to become active and extend their support.

Although Sitaula did not name anyone in his speech, his remarks appeared to be directed at former vice-president Purna Bahadur Khadka and leader Dr Shekhar Koirala. Both leaders have stayed away from the convention processes initiated by the two rival factions.

“Some of our capable and promising leaders appear to be remaining neutral at present. When there is a dispute within a party or a family, neutrality cannot lead us anywhere. You must express your views. If we have done something wrong, tell us,” Sitaula said.

The establishment faction led by Gagan Thapa held its 15th general convention in October. Meanwhile, the Deuba faction has launched a parallel convention process under the banner of the regular 15th general convention.

Khadka and Koirala have stayed out of both processes and remain separate from the factional contest. Koirala, meanwhile, is preparing to launch a nationwide campaign to bring the two divided factions together and restore party unity.

Stating that he wanted to build an independent, strong and progressive Nepal on the foundations of the party’s history, struggles and sacrifices, Sitaula questioned why some leaders had chosen to remain neutral.

“Why do you remain neutral in such a situation? Your neutrality has also created some problems for us. We want to see you active. We need your support,” he said.

Sitaula also expressed dissatisfaction with central leaders who had previously signed a statement declaring the special general convention wrong but gradually shifted towards supporting it.

He claimed that neither the looting, arson and vandalism of September 9 last year nor the special general convention could be justified on political, statutory or legal grounds.

He accused leaders who had taken control of the party headquarters in Sanepa through the special general convention of showing no courage, saying that their attempt to seize the party in haste had instead landed them in trouble.

title: Nepal-India economic partnership should not be hampered by political differences - OnlineKhabar English News
description: Nepal-India economic partnership should not be hampered by political differences  OnlineKhabar English News
publisher.title: OnlineKhabar English News
full_article:
The contemporary Nepal-India relationship must be understood in the context of a world in great turmoil. The multilateral system is increasingly disordered, conflicts and wars are continuing, and the global energy landscape is undergoing significant changes. Amid uncertainty over global oil and gas supplies, it is particularly important for neighbouring countries to work together and address shared challenges.

Despite these challenges, there are also opportunities to strengthen bilateral ties. Major political changes have taken place in Nepal over the past year.

The events of September 2025 and their aftermath have been described as a structural shift in traditional politics. New political forces have emerged, and a different generation of leaders has taken the reins of government. This is probably a once-in-a-generation moment of change.

I should clarify that I am speaking as an independent individual and do not represent any institution or government.

This new generation of leaders is young, talented and dynamic, with a focus on economic development and stability. Importantly, they do not carry the political baggage of the past.

There are always problems in any relationship, particularly one as close as that between India and Nepal. However, these should not hamper economic cooperation and partnership between the two countries.

People sometimes ask whether economic cooperation can move forward when so many bilateral problems remain unresolved. Given the nature of our relationship, I do not think there will ever be a time when all our problems are resolved. There will always be differences, but there will also be opportunities for partnership.

The challenge is to expand that partnership while addressing existing problems as far as possible. We should not allow bilateral difficulties to overshadow economic cooperation. Instead, both countries should focus on mutually beneficial opportunities in economic development and take practical steps to reduce inefficiencies in the relationship.

I believe this is broadly the thinking on both sides. These developments represent a moment of hope for Nepal and Nepal-India relations. Both governments and the people of the two countries should seize this opportunity and work towards strengthening the relationship.

Nepal’s prime minister is expected to visit India in the very near future. This will be his first visit, and although it may be short, it presents an important opportunity.

With new leadership in Nepal, it is essential for the leaders of both countries to understand each other. Personal interactions, face-to-face meetings and one-on-one conversations are important for building mutual understanding and trust.

Considerable groundwork has already been undertaken. I understand that most of the 42 bilateral mechanisms between the two countries have held meetings. The prime minister’s visit will therefore provide an opportunity not only for the two leaders to establish a rapport but also to take substantive decisions on pending issues.

Several important visits have already taken place ahead of the prime minister’s visit. We hope it will be a substantive and productive one.

Much has already been said about the priority areas for cooperation. I would reiterate General Anil Chauhan’s point that we need to move beyond aid, trade and investment towards creating value together.

This requires developing mechanisms to advance cooperation in emerging sectors, including information technology, connecting Nepal’s startup ecosystem with India’s, and addressing climate change.

Ranjit Rae

Climate issues have historically not been a prominent element of bilateral engagement. However, developments in both countries in recent years demonstrate how critical global warming and climate change have become.

Their impacts on people’s lives and livelihoods are increasingly evident. Beyond the immediate loss of lives and property, climate change also has implications for long-term development, including large dams and hydropower projects. Both countries must therefore find technical solutions to address these challenges, particularly those affecting water availability. Climate change must become an integral part of the bilateral agenda.

General Chauhan also mentioned humanitarian assistance and disaster relief (HADR). Drawing on my own experience, I would like to acknowledge the important role played by the two armies, which maintain a strong relationship.

Their cooperation in the aftermath of the 2015 earthquake was instrumental in addressing the devastating impact of the disaster. India also made a significant contribution to rehabilitation and reconstruction following the Bhotekoshi disaster.

India has already extended humanitarian assistance and disaster relief support, but there is further scope for cooperation in rehabilitation and reconstruction. The nature of India’s continued support could be an important subject of bilateral discussions.

Ambassador Vijay Kant Karna also referred to Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s proposal for a trilateral mechanism involving China, Nepal and India to address climate change and natural disasters. All three countries are affected by these challenges.

As a lower riparian country, India is inevitably affected by developments in upper riparian regions. I believe this is an interesting proposal, and although I do not know whether the Nepali side has developed it in detail, it is certainly worthy of consideration. The interests of all three countries converge on these issues, and the initiative should be taken forward.

The government has an important role in advancing bilateral relations, but the private sector and other stakeholders must also take advantage of the framework being created.

This framework includes connectivity in its broadest sense, encompassing digital and financial links, cross-border infrastructure, transmission lines and other forms of physical connectivity. Much of the necessary legal framework is already in place through bilateral agreements. The challenge now is to implement the projects.

During my tenure, I helped establish the first Joint Monitoring Group for Indian projects in Nepal. Such mechanisms can help address implementation challenges, including land acquisition, clearances and other procedural issues, particularly in road projects.

We need practical approaches to resolving these problems. When implementation difficulties remain unaddressed, they accumulate and lead to allegations that one side has failed to fulfil its responsibilities. A problem-solving approach can help prevent such situations and ensure that projects move forward.

Another important priority is establishing a long-term vision for the relationship. Although the two countries have numerous bilateral mechanisms, the time has come for their governments to agree on what they want to achieve in each sector over the long term.

This shared vision should be translated into action-oriented plans and strategies. These could be made public and monitored by both governments and other stakeholders, including the media.

It is equally important to establish clear targets. We already have a vision statement on energy that sets out what the two countries expect to achieve within a specified period. Similar targets should be established in other sectors, with regular assessments of progress. Where targets are not met, both sides should examine the reasons and identify the steps needed to address the shortcomings.

A pragmatic approach to economic partnership and cooperation would go a long way towards strengthening bilateral relations.

The regional dimension is also important. Some progress has been made towards developing a sub-regional energy grid, and agreements on motor vehicle movement have been reached among some countries in the region.

These initiatives should be strengthened to create an interconnected and open regional space in which every country has the opportunity to fully explore its comparative advantages.

title: Lawmaker BK warns of child exploitation in hotels, homes and brick kilns across Nepal - OnlineKhabar English News
description: Lawmaker BK warns of child exploitation in hotels, homes and brick kilns across Nepal  OnlineKhabar English News
publisher.title: OnlineKhabar English News
full_article:
Kathmandu, November 17

Nepali Communist Party lawmaker Parbati BK has said human trafficking is not limited to foreign countries, as women, workers and children are also being trafficked and exploited within Nepal.

Speaking at a meeting of the House of Representatives’ Women and Social Affairs Committee on Tuesday, where a proposed bill to control human trafficking and transportation was discussed, BK called for a timely revision of the law to address both domestic and international trafficking.

She said children from poor and working-class families were being brought from villages to cities with promises of education and a better future, only to be subjected to severe exploitation.

According to her, such children are often employed in hotels, restaurants and private households instead of being allowed to grow up with their families and receive an education.

She also drew the government’s attention to the continued exploitation of children in brick kilns. Recalling her own experience, she said she had rescued five children from Salyan who were working at a brick kiln in Lalitpur a year ago.

BK also highlighted organised human trafficking under the guise of foreign employment. She said brokers arrange everything from passports to overseas travel, and workers often realise they have been trafficked only after reaching their destination.

She urged lawmakers to ensure that the proposed legislation addresses these forms of exploitation, particularly those affecting women and workers.

title: French parliamentary delegation calls on NA Chair Dahal - The Rising Nepal
description: French parliamentary delegation calls on NA Chair Dahal  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Kathmandu, Nov 17: A French parliamentary delegation today paid a courtesy call on Chairperson of the National Assembly (NA), Narayan Prasad Dahal.

During the meeting held at the NA Chair's Office in Singha Durbar, matters relating to diplomatic relations between the two countries, mutual interests and parliamentary cooperation were discussed.

The French delegation is led by Beatrice Piron, President of France-Nepal Friendship Group under the lower house of the French parliament, according to the Secretariat of NA Chair.

On the occasion, Chair Dahal said the visit by the French parliamentary delegation has contributed to further strengthening bilateral and parliamentary ties.

Appraising the delegation that an-eight member Nepal-France Parliamentary Friendship Group has been formed under the federal parliament to expand the Nepal-France parliamentary relations, he expressed his hope that the parliamentary cooperation and exchange of experiences between the two countries would help further strengthen the diplomatic ties between the two countries.

He also expressed gratitude to France for its sympathy conveyed by the French President to Nepal following the August 26 devastating floods, its solidarity with Nepal during the crisis and support extended through the European Union.

Dahal expressed his sorrow over the families of four French citizens who went missing in the floods.

On the occasion, Beatrice Piron said this was her first visit to Nepal and was immensely impressed by the environment here.

Stating that France-Nepal Friendship Group has been established within the French Parliament, she emphasized the need to enhance the level of exchange of parliamentary practices through such groups.(RSS)

title: "Nobody Came To My Rescue": Amitabh Bachchan Recalls Nearly Drowning While Kayaking In Nepal - NDTV
description: "Nobody Came To My Rescue": Amitabh Bachchan Recalls Nearly Drowning While Kayaking In Nepal  NDTV
publisher.title: NDTV
full_article:
After facing some health concerns, Amitabh Bachchan is back as the host of Kaun Banega Crorepati 18 . In the latest episode, the veteran actor recalled the time he almost drowned while kayaking in Nepal.



Speaking to a contestant, Amitabh Bachchan revealed that while he was shooting for a film in Nepal, someone told him to go kayaking. The incident turned almost fatal for him.



Amitabh Bachchan Recalls Almost Drowning



Bachchan said that he was initially reluctant to go kayaking but decided to eventually do so. The actor recalled that the kayak was very narrow and he struggled to get into it for about 45 minutes.



Things got worse soon. The boat capsized while Bachchan was paddling. The actor added, “I was supposed to turn the boat one way, but I turned it the other way, and the boat capsized. When it overturned, I had been told that if such a situation arose, I should push my hands upwards from underwater so that the boat would right itself.”



The move did not work out. Instead of trying to get the boat upright again, Bachchan decided to attract the attention of people nearby. The Sholay star said he waved his hands around so that someone would realise he was almost drowning.



The actor described this experience as “frightening” and added that nobody came to his rescue for some time.



He explained, “You won't believe it, but nobody came to rescue me. On top of that, we were shooting a film, and the film's hero himself was drowning. Imagine they would have had to continue working with the other hero. However, someone standing near the waterfall realised that something was seriously wrong, and somehow managed to pull me out.”



Bachchan said that the experience was “quite an ordeal”. The actor mentioned that getting him out of the water “proved to be quite difficult” but people finally managed to help him.



Amitabh Bachchan's Upcoming Projects



Amitabh Bachchan is currently hosting Kaun Banega Crorepati 18 . He will feature next in Kalki 2, the sequel to director Nag Ashwin's sci-fi movie. The actor will also star in the upcoming courtroom drama Section 84.

title: Nepal Considers Bill to Allow Abortion at Any Gestation Stage, Sparking Debate - Ratopati
description: Nepal Considers Bill to Allow Abortion at Any Gestation Stage, Sparking Debate  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. As if a fetus is growing inside a mother's womb. Its limbs have started to move. It is capable of breathing. And, having taken a complete human form, it is now waiting to see the beautiful world.

Did you know? If a bill registered by the government is passed as is, the baby may not be guaranteed to see the beautiful world. If the provision mentioned in the bill, allowing termination of 'pregnancy of any duration', gets legal recognition, many accidents and risks could occur. If the provision is misused, even babies ready to be born could be killed inside the womb in the name of 'abortion'.

Yes, such a provision has been added to the 'Bill to Amend the Safe Motherhood and Reproductive Health Rights Act 2075, registered in Parliament on October 5, 2083 BS'. In Section 15(b1) of the proposal registered by Health and Food Sanitation Minister Nisha Mehta in the House of Representatives, the words 'pregnancy of any duration' have been replaced with 'pregnancy of twenty-eight weeks'. As a result, experts and stakeholders warn that legal loopholes will remain and its misuse could lead to extraordinary anomalies.

Obstetrician Dr. Jagdishwar Gautam said, 'We strongly object to the kind of law being made in Nepal. This is a law for killing people. Such a thing should not be done.'

Previously, under special circumstances, pregnancies up to 28 weeks could be terminated. Even though the fetus develops by 22 weeks, voices have been raised that the 28-week period is too long, and the preparation for a new provision of unlimited duration has generated heated debate.

The government's proposal for 'abortion of pregnancy of any duration', presented in the name of protecting the mother's health and right to self-determination, raises a serious question – is this protecting the mother's rights or a direct attack on the baby's right to live?

Many senior gynecologists and obstetricians have objected to the legal validity being given to terminate a fetus that has passed 28 weeks, or 196 days, in the name of abortion. They have strongly protested, calling it 'inhumane, insensitive, and potentially legalizing infanticide'. Such a bill has created serious ethical, legal, and medical ripples.

The government has moved forward with a bill allowing abortion of pregnancies of 'any duration' if an underage girl under 18 becomes pregnant due to rape or incest. The proposed bill has a flexible provision allowing abortion at any time with the advice of a licensed physician and the consent of the woman, if the fetus has a disability due to genetic or hereditary defects, or if not terminating the pregnancy poses a serious risk to the pregnant woman's life, physical or mental health, and there is a possibility of giving birth to a disabled child.

The reason given in the new bill for allowing abortion of 'any duration' is: 'If the pregnant woman's life is at risk, or if her physical or mental health deteriorates, or if the pregnancy is due to rape or incest of a girl under 18 years of age or a woman with a disability, or if the fetus has defects and is unlikely to survive after birth, or if the fetal development is impaired due to hereditary (genetic) defects or any other reason, abortion can be performed at any stage with the consent of the pregnant woman.'

However, many gynecologists and obstetricians have stated that this should be completely rejected, arguing that a pregnancy after 22 weeks is not an abortion but a 'delivery', and legalizing the killing of a fetus that is fully developed by 26 weeks and can breathe outside the womb. According to them, 'passing the proposed bill as is means snatching away the fundamental right to life of a baby and seeking to legalize infanticide.'

Former President of the Society of Gynecologists and Obstetricians of Nepal, Dr. Ganesh Dangal, warned that keeping abortions of fetuses over 20 weeks or weighing more than 500 grams legally open could create complex situations later. He argued that abortions beyond 20 weeks should not be taken lightly, as a fetus over 20 weeks or weighing more than 500 grams has a chance of survival and can be saved. He said, 'Abortions beyond 20 weeks should not be done. Because a fetus over 20 weeks or weighing 500 grams can be saved. Therefore, I feel that abortions beyond this duration should not be done.'

He emphasized that procedures adopted in special health conditions, such as when the mother's health is at extreme risk, or when the baby has incurable diseases or underdeveloped heart, should be called 'delivery by medical means' rather than abortion.

Lawyer Sabin Shrestha mentioned that the law already gives the right to choose up to 12 weeks in normal circumstances, and it is not appropriate to open abortion without a time limit in all situations. He stated that abortion should not be allowed at any duration in normal circumstances. Regarding the proposed provision in the bill to 'allow abortion at any duration', he clarified that abortion is not just a woman's right to self-determination.

According to lawyer Shrestha, the proposed amendment bill envisages abortion of any duration only in three specific and complex situations, not in all circumstances. He argued that abortion at any stage is envisioned only in cases where the pregnant woman's life is at risk, the fetus has a disability or has died in the womb, or in cases of pregnancy resulting from rape or incest of a minor under 18 years of age. He clarified that the removal of the time limit in such limited circumstances is an attempt to address the bitter reality of the past where even an 11-year-old girl had to give birth due to legal complications.

Shrestha pointed out that although the existing law provides for strict punishment for abortion based on sex identification, the fact that not a single case has been filed so far indicates weak law enforcement. He emphasized the need for timely decisions as abortions performed later are risky, and suggested that regulatory bodies like the Family Welfare Division should strictly monitor and evaluate registered health institutions and doctors to prevent misuse of the law.

Abortion Status

While assessing the risks of removing the duration limit, it is also necessary to look at the existing status and statistics of abortion in Nepal.

According to the National Health Demographic Survey 2022, 10 percent of women voluntarily aborted their pregnancies in the last three years, while 9 percent experienced spontaneous abortion (miscarriage).

Based on age groups, women aged 25 to 29, who have the highest reproductive capacity, have the highest rate of voluntary abortion (15 per 1,000 women).

Similarly, 12 per 1,000 women aged 20 to 24 and 11 per 1,000 women aged 30 to 34 have undergone voluntary abortion.

What are the risks?

Experts and doctors argue that since surveys show a significant portion of total pregnancies end in voluntary abortion, the phrase 'any duration' could encourage uncontrolled practices. They have drawn attention to the complications that may arise from opening up 'any duration' without clear procedures, strict criteria, or specific limits.

'While removing the time limit for abortion in special circumstances (such as rape of girls under 18, risk to the mother's life, or severe fetal abnormalities) is humane and practically necessary, legal loopholes should not be left in the abortion of fully developed living fetuses.' They emphasize the need for clear procedures, strict regulatory mechanisms, and multi-physician opinions to balance the mother's right to self-determination and the baby's right to live, and to prevent misuse.

Obstetrician Dr. Jagdishwar Gautam said that abortion should not be performed after 22 weeks. He stated that abortion after 22 weeks should not be called abortion, but delivery.

In a video message on social media Facebook, he said, 'In developed countries, babies after 22 weeks survive, and even here, babies after 26 weeks are surviving. I have saved hundreds of babies at 26, 27, 28 weeks. Therefore, this is delivery.'

Gautam said that if the baby is abnormal for any reason, delivery or abortion can be done at any time. However, if the mother is fine, abortion should not be done after 22 weeks in such a situation.

Dr. Gautam said, 'After 22 weeks, the baby is born alive. Doctors work to save, not to kill. And the kind of law being made in Nepal. We strongly object to this law. This is a law for killing people. Such a thing should not be done.'

He argued that it is not known for what reason the mother conceived the child in her womb, whether it was rape, incest, or something else. He said, 'We listen to the mother, but not to the baby in the womb? We must listen to the voices of the voiceless. Therefore, the law that allows abortion at any week is directly unethical and unscientific.'

Former President Dr. Dangal said that the provision allowing abortion at any duration would be very liberal and should not be normalized. He suggested that after the act comes into force, the regulations should have a clear monitoring mechanism and should not have any 'loopholes' that could lead to misuse.

He emphasized that the regulations should include the mandatory opinion of two or more doctors and clearly specify special circumstances to provide legal clarity.

Obstetrician Dr. Kirtipal Subedi said that to prevent misuse such as sex-selective abortion or undue pressure on doctors due to the relaxation of time limits, strict legal provisions and effective regulatory mechanisms are necessary. He said, 'Strict legal provisions and effective regulatory mechanisms are necessary to prevent the risk of misuse. Keeping in mind international practices and Nepal's limited health infrastructure, a clear protocol should be established with the opinion of at least two specialists, police documents, and medical evidence.'

Dr. Subedi said that if clear laws and strict monitoring are implemented, doctors will be able to provide services with confidence, and on the other hand, no woman will be deprived of safe health services.

Arguments Vary

According to the proposed bill, victims of rape under 18 may have to undergo late abortions due to legal, social, and psychological pressure. Some obstetricians and gynecologists argue that abortion rules should be somewhat flexible, considering the physical and mental sensitivity of minors. According to them, based on the proposed bill, medical termination of pregnancies of 24 or 34 weeks may become necessary.

There is a high possibility that the baby will be born alive during an abortion or termination at such a late stage. If the baby is born alive in such a situation, the minor herself will not be in a position to take responsibility or guardianship. The lack of clarity in the law regarding who will take responsibility for such babies born in special circumstances like rape or incest has created confusion.

Dr. Padmaraj Pant, President of the Society of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, argues that the new bill proposes a legal provision to allow abortion at any time if the mother's life is at risk or if the fetus in the womb has a severe congenital defect or disability. He claims that previously, due to the 28-week limitation, abortions were not allowed even in such complex situations, and there was a risk of legal punishment, but now this legal complexity has been eased to create a safe environment for both service providers and recipients. He expects this provision to contribute to reducing maternal and infant mortality and saving women facing complex health problems from premature death.

Dr. Samir Kumar Adhikari, spokesperson for the Ministry of Health, said that the bill has been introduced based on past experiences and studies. He said, 'The bill has been presented based on all studies and experiences. The procedure will cover all aspects later.'

Nirdesh Vaidya, associate professor of public health, said that making abortion more lenient requires effective control of issues such as sex-selective abortion and abortion by unmarried couples. He said, 'To manage this, public health and sex education programs should reach the school level and adolescents. Concrete strategies should be adopted to reduce teenage pregnancy.'

He stated that clear protocols should be established for doctors and health institutions providing safe abortion services, monitoring should be strengthened, and the law should be properly implemented keeping in mind the human rights of both mother and child.

What is Abortion? What is 'Delivery'?

According to the World Health Organization, abortion is defined as the termination of pregnancy before 22 weeks of gestation or with a fetal weight of less than 500 grams. The birth of a live infant in the weeks following, from 22 weeks up to 37 weeks, is considered premature birth. The 22-week period or 500-gram weight is considered the minimum limit for fetal survival outside the womb in medical science. These scientific and technical parameters are officially used in the medical and health fields to clearly distinguish between abortion and premature birth.

Similarly, according to the World Health Organization and medical science, an infant born after completing 37 weeks and up to 42 weeks of gestation is considered a full-term infant.

What was in the past? What is in the proposal?

According to the Safe Motherhood and Reproductive Health Rights Act 2075, 'abortion' was defined as the expulsion or removal of the fetus from the uterus before it is naturally viable. The proposed provision modifies this to define 'abortion' as the act of removing the fetus from the uterus before it is naturally viable. Similarly, regarding 'abortion services', the previous act stated that it is a service provided by a licensed health worker in a licensed health institution after completing the procedures as per this act.

The proposed provision states that abortion services should be provided by health institutions and health workers registered for providing abortion services as per Section 18, Sub-section (1) of the prevailing law.

Previously, services could be provided by other trained midwives or health workers in government and community health institutions due to a lack of skilled health workers. However, the new provision proposes that all types of health institutions must provide delivery services only through skilled health workers or trained midwives.

Suggestions from the Society of Specialists

The Nepal Society of Obstetricians and Gynecologists has presented its official opinions and suggestions on some sections and provisions of the Bill to Amend the Safe Motherhood and Reproductive Health Rights Act, 2075, to the Parliamentary Committee on Education, Health, and Information Technology. The society has pointed out that ambiguities in various sections of the act could create difficulties for doctors and health workers in providing services.

Section 1(d) of the bill defines abortion as the act of removing the fetus from the uterus before it is naturally viable. Clarifying this from a scientific and practical perspective, the society has demanded that abortion and delivery be distinguished according to the duration of the pregnancy. It has been stated that if the difference between abortion, which is the termination of pregnancy up to the point of fetal viability, and delivery, which occurs after 20 to 24 weeks, is not clearly defined, legal complications may arise.

Similarly, Section 15(b1) of the proposed bill allows safe abortion of any duration in case of pregnancy resulting from rape or incest of girls under 18 years of age. The society has stated that it is necessary to adopt flexibility in abortion rules, considering the physical and mental sensitivity of minors. Furthermore, it has been suggested that when a pregnancy of 24 or 34 weeks is medically terminated, there is a high possibility of the baby being born alive, and therefore, clear legal provisions should be made regarding the responsibility and management of such infants, as the minor herself cannot be a guardian.

The society has also expressed concern about the provision in Section 16(c) of the bill, which states that if a child is born alive during an abortion and dies as a result, it will be considered forced abortion. It has been demanded that clear legal provisions should be made to ensure that health workers are not held criminally liable for forced abortion in cases where a child is born alive due to natural complications and accidental events and later dies. Emphasis has been placed on not holding healthcare providers liable for complications arising during treatment due to maternal health risks such as eclampsia.

Regarding the provision of safe abortion services in Section 18(1), it is stated that health institutions and health workers licensed under prevailing law must be 'registered' as specified to provide safe abortion services. The society has suggested that including the word 'registered' in the act could create practical and legal complications for doctors, and therefore, flexibility should be incorporated in the act, with detailed provisions strictly included in the regulations.

Section 25(c)(1) proposes punishment for causing risk or harm due to not referring to another health institution. It has been argued that this provision could create legal fear among health workers and make it difficult to work in institutions with fewer resources, as it should only be considered an offense if treatment is possible in one's own institution and referral is made knowingly to another institution. Therefore, the society has specifically requested that clear criteria be included in the regulations regarding when treatment is possible and when referral is necessary.

title: Explained: Nepal and India have revived stalled air route talks. Here’s what you need to know - The Kathmandu Post
description: Explained: Nepal and India have revived stalled air route talks. Here’s what you need to know  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
After a three-year break, Nepal and India have resumed talks to resolve longstanding disputes over cross-border air routes, an issue that has remained entangled in bilateral politics and geopolitical tensions since 2009.

The two countries have repeatedly attempted to settle the issue, but frequent changes of government, security concerns, and strained diplomatic relations have prevented a breakthrough.

Nepal is now pushing to make the L626 (Kathmandu-Mahendranagar) route in western Nepal a two-way air corridor, allowing international aircraft to enter and leave through the western border, according to tourism ministry officials.

The route began operating on November 19, 2009, one-way to exit.

Jay Narayan Acharya, spokesperson for the Tourism Ministry, who is currently in New Delhi, said Nepal had prioritised securing two-way operation of the route. Nepal hopes for an agreement during Prime Minister Balendra Shaha’s Delhi visit next week.

The L626 route connects Kathmandu to Delhi via Mahendranagar in Nepal and Pantnagar in India. It is 20 miles shorter than the existing B345 (Bhairahawa-Lucknow-Delhi) route, which is also a one-way departure route. The L626 allows airlines to use 291 nautical miles (539 kilometres) of Nepali airspace, compared with just 100 nautical miles (185 kilometres) along the B345 route.

Greater use of Nepali airspace would generate additional revenue for the country while reducing flight distances and operating costs. According to officials at the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal, depending on aircraft size, Nepal can generate $250-$500 per aircraft for using Nepali airspace.

Here is what you need to know about the air route dispute.

When did the issue begin?

Nepal has been pressing India for additional international air entry routes since 2009, after deciding to build international airports in Pokhara and Bhairahawa.

The issue received political backing during Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit to Nepal in August 2014.

Nepal proposed three new entry points through Janakpur, Bhairahawa and Nepalgunj.

Bhairahawa-based Gautam Buddha International Airport SHUTTERSTOCK

A joint communiqué issued after the visit stated that opening direct cross-border entry routes at Janakpur, Bhairahawa and Nepalgunj would facilitate flights between Pokhara, Bhairahawa, and Lucknow, reduce travel time and costs, and improve air connectivity between the two countries.

The two prime ministers, Sushil Koirala and Narendra Modi, subsequently directed their respective authorities to resolve the issue within six months. However, the commitment was never fulfilled.

In 2016, Nepal and India agreed to make the L626 (Kathmandu-Mahendranagar) route two-way, following an assessment that it would benefit both countries and facilitate the future development of the Trans-Himalaya 2 route (Kathmandu-Bagdogra-Guwahati-Silchar-Imphal-Kunming).

India, however, said it needed further internal consultations before making a final decision.

New Delhi had long expressed reservations about opening entry points through Bhairahawa and Nepalgunj, citing security concerns linked to the strategic Gorakhpur air base, where fighter jet exercises are regularly conducted.

In February 2017, the two countries agreed to form a joint technical team to examine the feasibility of opening the three proposed routes.

Until April 2018, India had remained positive about opening western entry routes after a technical team was formed to address safety concerns.

However, bilateral relations deteriorated after Kathmandu withdrew from a joint military exercise with BIMSTEC countries in Pune in September 2018, despite initially agreeing to participate.

India expressed dissatisfaction over Nepal's withdrawal, particularly within its defence establishment.

That same year, Nepal participated in the second Nepal-China joint military exercise, Sagarmatha Friendship-2, in China's Sichuan province, further complicating bilateral defence sensitivities.

Discussions on the safety assessment of the proposed air routes subsequently stalled.

Officials say India's position later hardened. Meetings were held in 2019 and again in 2023, but neither produced a breakthrough.

Nepal has consistently argued that expanding cross-border air routes is essential because almost all inbound international air traffic depends on the Simara entry point.

In contrast, aircraft departing Nepal have access to seven exit points—Bhairahawa and Mahendranagar in the west; and Simara, Biratnagar, Tumlingtar, Mechi and Janakpur in the east.

Two additional entry points over Mechi and Tumlingtar (NONIM), used by aircraft arriving from Bhutan and Lhasa respectively, also exist but handle limited traffic.

As a result, Simara remains heavily congested.

How have the restrictions affected the new international airports?

The lack of western entry routes has undermined the commercial viability of Gautam Buddha International Airport in Bhairahawa and Pokhara International Airport, projects on which Nepal has spent more than Rs60 billion combined.

The air traffic control room at Gautam Buddha International Airport in Bhairahawa. Post File Photo

Gautam Buddha International Airport was upgraded as Nepal's second international airport on May 16, 2022, while Pokhara International Airport was inaugurated on January 1, 2023 as the third international gateway.

For a long time, both airports failed to attract scheduled international passenger services, handling only occasional charter flights.

On September 25 this year, flydubai launched daily scheduled non-stop flights between Dubai International Airport and Pokhara International Airport, establishing the first direct air link between Dubai and western Nepal.

Air entry routes are considered critical for both airports.

For example, an aircraft flying to Bhairahawa from the west cannot enter Nepal directly over Bhairahawa, Nepalgunj or Mahendranagar. Instead, it must make a roughly 300-kilometre detour to enter Nepal through Simara in the east before flying back west.

Experts say the longer route increases fuel consumption and operating costs, making flights more expensive, particularly flights from New Delhi.

Tourism Ministry documents show that international flights to Pokhara from the west must fly an additional 185 kilometres if new cross-border air entry routes are not opened.

Were air routes the only reason the airports failed to attract flights?

No. Officials familiar with the matter say the lack of marketing by Nepal's civil aviation body was also a major reason the new airports failed to attract international airlines.

Two former officials from the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal said the air route issue had been used to explain away shortcomings in promoting the airports.

"To hide the shortcomings, a narrative was built that due to the air route problems, Bhairahawa and Pokhara failed to attract flights," they said. "If the problem was for flights coming from the west, for example, New Delhi, both airports had no problems on the route for flights coming from the east, for example, Japan, South Korea, Dhaka and even Kolkata."

Of the 28 international airlines connecting Nepal, half enter the country through the east.

"So, it's not logical to say that the air route was the sole problem that kept international airlines off route to Bhairahawa and Pokhara," the former officials said.

The check-in counter at Pokhara International Airport. Post File Photo

"There was zero marketing to promote the new airports," said a Tourism Ministry official who wished not to be named. "We cannot just blame the route as there was a wider option to draw flights from East Asian countries. Airports basically have to create demand. Once there is competition, airlines come and operate. That's a global trend. Nepal, however, failed to market its new facility.”

What happened during the 2023 talks?

India agreed to allow inbound flights to use the L626 route, entering Nepal from the west over Mahendranagar, but only at altitudes between 15,000 and 24,000 feet. Aviation experts said the restriction was too low for jet aircraft.

The agreement, however, was never formalised.

India had already approved this air entry route in 2018 for low-level flights. It was operationally feasible for ATR-type aircraft.

Jet aircraft generally achieve better fuel efficiency at higher cruising altitudes, where the air is colder and thinner. At a given indicated airspeed and lift condition, aircraft travel faster through the air while their engines generally consume less fuel than at lower altitudes.

However, the 2023 discussions produced one breakthrough.

The then Prime Minister Pushpa Kamal Dahal said after his India visit that the southern neighbour had agreed to a "near-border operation" agreement.

Under such an arrangement, aircraft can enter each other's airspace in emergencies, such as when deteriorating weather conditions require them to divert to a nearby airport. Neighbouring countries generally sign such agreements to ensure safe aircraft operations near their borders. The agreement would facilitate the Gautam Buddha Airport, close to the border and frequent overlapping was one of the problems.

The proposed near-border operation agreement has now been revived.

"We sent the draft agreement to our counterpart in India two months ago through the Foreign Ministry," a Tourism Ministry official said. "We are waiting for the response."

In July this year , the bilateral air route issue was discussed during a meeting between Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal and Munu Mahawar, additional secretary at India's Ministry of External Affairs, in Kathmandu.

Pokhara International Airport officially opened and began operations on January 1, 2023. Shutterstock

Mahawar was in Nepal to attend the 13th Nepal-India Joint Steering Committee meeting at the energy secretary level, which concluded in Pokhara.

What is the issue involving Bagdogra Airport?

India has formally requested Nepal to sign a near-border operation agreement for Bagdogra airport, which serves the city of Siliguri in West Bengal. Nepal has sought a similar arrangement for Bhairahawa airport.

The Tourism Ministry received the formal request from the Indian Embassy in Kathmandu on Tuesday.

"In case of an emergency, for instance, if the weather deteriorates, the agreement provides a protection area for aircraft to fly safely," ministry officials said.

The two requests have brought the near-border operation arrangement back into bilateral discussions, although the two countries have yet to finalise the agreement.

How have geopolitical tensions affected the air route issue?

Officials say Nepal's two new international airports have also become caught in regional geopolitical competition.

Pokhara International Airport was built with Chinese financing, while a Chinese contractor constructed Gautam Buddha International Airport in Bhairahawa.

India has withheld landing permits for Himalaya Airlines to fly to New Delhi since 2015 because the airline is owned by a Chinese company, according to officials familiar with the matter.

India has also made clear that it will not purchase electricity from hydropower projects in Nepal involving Chinese investment. Insiders say the airports have faced similar geopolitical sensitivities.

This was evident on May 16, 2022, when visiting Indian Prime Minister Modi flew over the newly built international airport in Bhairahawa during its inauguration and landed in Lumbini instead.

Another Tourism Ministry official said India had refused to grant operating authorisation to Buddha Air to fly from Pokhara to Lucknow, citing a "diplomatic issue".

During a visit by then Prime Minister Dahal to India in June 2023, Indian Foreign Secretary Vinay Mohan Kwatra acknowledged that air connectivity between the two countries had been discussed.

"There are many elements to it. There are elements to connect different cities of Nepal with different cities in India through different air routes," Kwatra told journalists in New Delhi.

He said technical experts would examine the proposals and make appropriate decisions.

"These are questions which require extensive technical examinations…at some point, the airspace is under the domains which are commanded by the air force," he added.

full_article:
Nepali youth climate activists have urged Australia, which holds the COP31 presidency, to push for grant-based climate finance and fair access to the loss and damage fund for countries like Nepal.

In a meeting with Australian officials in Antalya, Turkey, organised by People’s Movement for Climate Justice Nepal, the activists said countries that have contributed little to the climate crisis should not have to take on more debt to rebuild after climate-induced disasters. Climate finance, they said, is a matter of historical responsibility and justice, not charity.

The Australian side included officials from the climate change and energy ministry, the official overseeing consultations with observer groups and multilateral stakeholders, and the lead negotiator on loss and damage.

Photo: Courtesy of Arnab Chaudhary

“We presented their positions on the COP31 negotiating text, the work programme on climate finance, adaptation and mitigation,” said Arnab Chaudhary, a Nepali climate activist who attended the meeting.

He added that the group demanded adequate, needs-based funding for the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage; grants instead of loans for climate-vulnerable countries; and direct, easy access to climate finance for least developed countries and affected communities. They also called for transparency and accountability in how money is distributed, and for the fund’s guidance, grievance and reporting systems to work for affected communities.

The activists also briefed the officials on a petition campaign seeking grant-based finance to rebuild climate-hit communities in Nepal. It will be submitted to the UNFCCC, the World Bank, the loss and damage fund and the Nepal government.

Photo: Courtesy of Arnab Chaudhary

According to Chaudhary, the Australian officials said they would try to facilitate the demands in the negotiations. They advised the youth to keep lobbying other delegations, parties and observer groups, and noted that Nepal could seek technical support for post-disaster recovery through the Santiago Network, which provides technical assistance on loss and damage to climate-vulnerable developing countries. The officials also described the youth’s engagement as strategic rather than symbolic, the activists said.

description: Nepal Seeks Additional Air Routes from India Amidst Strategic Discussions  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. Among the issues that are always at the center of discussion and interest before almost every Prime Minister of Nepal's visit to India is the international air route between the two countries.

Although Nepal has been demanding additional air entry points from India for more than a decade, it has not reached a concrete conclusion. In the context of recent signals that India might grant an air route from Mahendranagar in return for a request for an entry point from Bagdogra, what are the real conditions, possibilities, and challenges of Nepal's aviation sector? Rato Pati has discussed this topic with former Director General of the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal (CANA), Rajkumar Khatri.

In the context of the Prime Minister's visit to India, the issue of air routes (air routes) is always raised. This time too, there are signals that India will ask for an entry route from Bagdogra and Nepal will be given a route from Mahendranagar or Bhairahawa. As someone who has worked in leadership positions in the aviation sector for a long time, how do you view the historical background of the air route that Nepal has been demanding from India and the current possibilities?

– Nepal's demand for an air entry route through Mahendranagar in India is not new; this issue has been raised for about 10 to 12 years. In fact, we have been demanding four air entry routes from India: Mahendranagar, Bhairahawa, Nepalgunj, and Janakpur. However, India has always postponed it, citing its security sensitivities. Specifically, the Indian side argues that there would be 'security threats' due to the Air Force base in India's Gorakhpur region and other strategic structures.

When I myself was the Director General of the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal, I had direct dialogues and discussions with Indian officials on this matter. In the discussions at that time, they complained that there was no other problem in giving us the route, but only some complexities in terms of security and air traffic safety. However, I still remember that when Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited Nepal, he took this issue seriously and publicly committed that the air route would be implemented within the next six months. I was working in Civil Aviation at that time.

But unfortunately, about 12 years have passed since that commitment was made, and it has not materialized to this day. Now, again, in the context of the Prime Minister's visit, the signal that the Mahendranagar route will be opened, if it is truly implemented, will definitely bring multifaceted and far-reaching benefits to Nepal.

What is the current status of international air travel in Nepal? Which entry points are currently used by aircraft coming to Nepal from various parts of the world, and what is the compulsion of using India's airspace?

Looking at the current state of international air entry points into Nepal, our airspace appears to be quite limited and dependent on a single point. Especially for all international aircraft coming to Nepal from the west, south, and the Middle East, 'Simara' is currently the only available entry point through India's airspace. Any aircraft coming from Europe, Gulf countries, or other Western countries must pass through India's airspace to enter Nepal, and there is no other option besides Simara.

Not only that, but aircraft coming from China also have to enter near Kakadvitta in eastern Nepal and then proceed to Simara instead of landing directly at Kathmandu airport, and then circle back to land at Kathmandu airport. Besides this, all other international airlines coming via India's airspace must use Simara as their entry and exit point. Apart from managing our own internal airspace, India has not provided any other entry point besides Simara for international flights using Indian airspace, thus Nepal's entire international aviation system is confined to the narrow scope of a single entry point.

What are the technical, time, and economic losses incurred when aircraft coming from West Asia, Europe, or the West have to come via Simara? How does this affect airline companies?

With only one Simara entry point, airline companies are bearing an extremely heavy technical and economic burden. Let's understand this with a simple example.

Suppose an aircraft is coming to Nepal from the Middle East or Europe, passing near Nepal's western airspace. If the Mahendranagar route were open, that aircraft could enter directly from western Nepal and land in Bhairahawa or Pokhara within minutes. But in the current situation, even an aircraft coming from the west has to travel all the way east to Simara via India, parallel to Nepal's western airspace. Then, an aircraft that needs to go to Bhairahawa or Pokhara has to circle back west after entering Simara. This is a paradoxical situation.

Flying for 25 minutes longer than the scheduled time directly affects the aircraft's maintenance schedule and the crew's duty hours. It is precisely this unnecessary time and high operating cost that has led foreign airline companies to show reluctance in flying to the airports built in the western and central regions of Nepal, as circling via Simara would result in significant commercial losses for them.

Thus, having to unnecessarily go to Simara and return wastes about 20 to 25 minutes of extra time on each flight. In the field of aviation, a delay of 20 to 25 minutes is a significant loss. On one hand, passengers and aircraft time are wasted, and on the other hand, the aircraft's fuel consumption increases significantly.

In today's competitive aviation market, fuel cost is the biggest expense for airline companies. Moreover, the technical operating life of the aircraft and the crew's flight hours also have a certain limit. Flying for 25 minutes longer than the scheduled time directly affects the aircraft's maintenance schedule and the crew's duty hours. It is precisely this unnecessary time and high operating cost that has led foreign airline companies to show reluctance in flying to the airports built in the western and central regions of Nepal, as circling via Simara would result in significant commercial losses for them.

Nepal had demanded four air routes from India. But now only the Mahendranagar route is being discussed more. Even if only Mahendranagar is given immediately without giving the routes for Bhairahawa, Nepalgunj, and Janakpur, how much benefit will it bring to Nepal?

Certainly, in the past, we had demanded all four air entry points from India: Mahendranagar, Bhairahawa, Nepalgunj, and Janakpur, and in principle, obtaining all those routes would be even better for Nepal. However, looking at the current diplomatic dialogue and my understanding of the situation, it does not seem that the Indian side will be ready to grant all four routes immediately. Rather, India appears to be more positive and agreeable to granting the air entry route from Mahendranagar in the immediate term. Discussions and dialogues on the remaining three routes will continue gradually in the future.

But the reality is that if India grants us only the entry route from Mahendranagar immediately, it will be a matter of great benefit for Nepal and the Nepali aviation sector. This is because Mahendranagar is the most strategic and shortest entry gate for flights coming from the west, Europe, and the Middle East. Once Mahendranagar is opened, the compulsion of taking the long detour via Simara will end. This will specifically breathe life into the operation of international airports in the western region.

For aircraft coming from the eastern region, i.e., Thailand, Bangkok, or Malaysia, the route naturally falls near the eastern or southern Simara, so there is not much difference. However, for the Middle East and European markets, which are our main international air traffic and where migrant workers and tourists travel, opening the Mahendranagar route will prove to be a sufficient and revolutionary step.

If India opens the Mahendranagar air route, how can the Gautam Buddha International Airport in Bhairahawa and the Pokhara International Airport, which are currently non-operational and idle, become operational?

The opening of the Mahendranagar route is like a lifeline for the Bhairahawa and Pokhara international airports. The Bhairahawa and Pokhara airports, built with billions of investments, are almost idle due to the lack of regular international flights. The main reason why foreign airline companies are not interested in flying to these two airports is the extra time, fuel cost, and commercial loss incurred by having to circle via Simara. When the route for direct entry from Mahendranagar opens, aircraft coming from the Middle East and Europe will be able to land directly in Bhairahawa and Pokhara without going to Simara.

This will save airline companies 25 minutes of time and a large amount of fuel, making flights to Bhairahawa and Pokhara commercially profitable for them. Especially, the Bhairahawa airport has the potential to operate at an even faster pace and more effectively than Pokhara. The availability of the Mahendranagar route will generate interest among foreign airlines, and they will be ready to operate regular flights. Furthermore, the full operation of Bhairahawa and Pokhara will greatly help in reducing the excessive air traffic pressure at Kathmandu's Tribhuvan International Airport. However, opening the route is not the only solution; we also need to be able to sell those airports commercially, i.e., market them effectively.

What other internal preparations and improvements need to be made by the Nepali government for the marketing and passenger attraction of the Bhairahawa and Pokhara airports after obtaining the Mahendranagar route?

Obtaining an air route is a technical aspect, but for the airport to operate sustainably, there must be a guarantee of passengers and business. Let's take the Bhairahawa airport as an example. The largest segment of passengers traveling from Nepal to the Middle East, i.e., the Gulf countries, consists of Nepali migrant workers going abroad for employment. Currently, migrant workers from western Nepal are compelled to come to Kathmandu to visit manpower companies, undergo health check-ups, obtain labor permits, and complete other administrative procedures. When the work is done in Kathmandu, they do not return to take a flight from Bhairahawa; they fly from Kathmandu.

Therefore, if the Government of Nepal provides all government and private services related to foreign employment, such as labor offices, manpower branches, medical centers, and visa facilitation mechanisms, in the Bhairahawa and Butwal areas, not a single migrant worker from the western region will have to come to Kathmandu. They will be able to fly easily from Bhairahawa.

Only after ensuring passenger traffic in this way will foreign airline companies schedule regular flights there. And, on the other hand, the government and tourism sector bodies must play an active role in promoting tourism in Pokhara and Bhairahawa, ensuring easy access to hotels and transportation, and strong marketing of those airports internationally. If these internal homeworks are completed, Nepal can fully leverage the benefits of the Mahendranagar route.

There is a discussion that India has asked for an entry point from Bagdogra in the east instead of or along with Mahendranagar. It is heard that the Nepali delegation has said that they will respond only after studying this matter in Nepal. What kind of impact could granting India an entry point from Bagdogra have on Nepal's security or air travel?

A final decision has not yet been made regarding Bagdogra, and it is a natural diplomatic process for the Nepali delegation to say they will decide after returning to Nepal and studying the technical aspects. However, based on my long experience in the aviation sector, I do not think that granting India an entry point from Bagdogra will pose a significant security threat or problem to Nepal. From a security perspective, there is no situation where such a serious challenge would arise from Indian flights over Nepal. The main question is whether Indian aircraft entering from Bagdogra will disturb Nepal's internal or international flights, which is a technical matter.

In my understanding, it does not seem that India will bring a large number of its aircraft into Nepal's airspace from Bagdogra. Possibly, India might have requested a small portion of Bagdogra only for facilitating flights in a specific and limited area of Bihar state. However, as I am no longer in an executive role and do not have the actual current air traffic data before me, the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal and aviation experts will surely conduct a thorough technical study and evaluation. If the technical study by the experts shows that granting entry from Bagdogra will not significantly affect Nepal's air safety and internal flight management, and if we get the Mahendranagar air entry point in return, it will be a very beneficial agreement for Nepal. In diplomacy, one should not hesitate to 'give and take' for mutual benefit.

Besides air routes, there are many other issues in Nepal's aviation sector. There are complaints that India has not provided necessary support to the Pokhara and Bhairahawa airports and that there is inequality in air connectivity between Nepal and India. What could be other major aviation sector agendas that Nepal should raise during this visit?

Certainly, not just air routes, but Nepal should also raise the issue of 'air connectivity', i.e., bilateral flight access, with India with equal vigor in the dialogue. As far as the discussion about India not cooperating with the Pokhara airport is concerned, the root of that is mainly this air route itself. The problem in connectivity seems to have arisen precisely because India has not granted this route. If India opens the Mahendranagar route, many connectivity problems will automatically find a solution, and we can expand connectivity with other countries as well.

Therefore, if the Government of Nepal provides all government and private services related to foreign employment, such as labor offices, manpower branches, medical centers, and visa facilitation mechanisms, in the Bhairahawa and Butwal areas, not a single migrant worker from the western region will have to come to Kathmandu. They will be able to fly easily from Bhairahawa.

And, a more serious and direct issue is the lack of flight permits for Nepali airline companies to fly to major Indian cities, including Delhi. Currently, there is significant inequality in flight permits between Nepal and India. Nepal has welcomed all types of Indian government and private airlines with open arms. We have granted as many flight permits as possible to Indian airlines like Indigo, Air India, etc., to fly to Kathmandu and elsewhere without any restrictions. But in return, India has not allowed private Nepali airline companies to fly to Delhi.

This unequal treatment must be ended, and the Government of Nepal must raise this issue seriously at the diplomatic level.

What is the actual situation regarding Nepali airline companies not being able to access Indian airspace and airports?

Looking at the current reality, only the national flag carrier Nepal Airlines Corporation (RNAC) has received permission to fly from Nepal to India's capital, Delhi. Capable and large private airline companies in Nepal have not been able to get permission to fly to Delhi, even though they want to. For example, Buddha Air has been trying to fly to Delhi for a long time, but India has only granted permission for Varanasi, not Delhi. This permission has not been granted to date.

Similarly, Shree Airlines has also been trying for a long time with full preparation for flights to Delhi. It is heard that assurances have been given verbally by the Indian side that Shree Airlines will be granted permission, but official written documents have not yet been received.

Thus, Nepali private airline companies are forced to sit idle, unable to fly internationally despite investing heavily, because India has not granted them flight permits. Meanwhile, Indian airlines are unilaterally capturing the market in Nepal. Even if a large private company in Nepal brings a new aircraft and wants to operate flights to major Indian cities, there is uncertainty about whether India will grant slots and permits. According to the principle of reciprocity, just as Nepal has welcomed Indian airlines openly, India should also grant Nepali private airlines easy flight permits to major destinations like Delhi.

This issue must be raised as a priority during high-level government visits.

India is the main source of Nepal's tourism market. If Nepali airline companies get easy access to cities like Delhi and the Mahendranagar route opens, what impact will it have on Nepal's overall tourism and economy?

As you said, the main and sustainable source market for our tourism industry is neighboring India. India has a large middle-class population that wants to come to Nepal for travel and religious tourism. When air connectivity between Nepal and India strengthens, i.e., when private sector airlines like Buddha Air and Shree Airlines, along with Indian aircraft, are allowed to fly from cities like Delhi, the number of flights and seat capacity will increase significantly. With healthy competition in the market, airfares will naturally become cheaper.

Currently, due to limited flights, the Kathmandu-Delhi airfare is extremely expensive, which makes some tourists hesitate to come by air even if they want to. As soon as fares become cheaper and flights become easier, the arrival of Indian tourists to Nepal will increase unprecedentedly.

Similarly, after the opening of the Mahendranagar route, tourists from Europe and the Middle East will also be able to come directly to Pokhara and Bhairahawa (Lumbini) in a shorter time and at a lower cost. This will bring a significant positive ripple effect to Nepal's tourism business, hotel industry, travel agencies, and the local economy. Overall, the improvement in air routes and air connectivity has the potential to take Nepal's tourism and economy to new heights.

India's proposed Bagdogra route should be immediately subjected to a detailed technical study by the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal and a team of aviation experts. If it does not have any significant impact on Nepal's air traffic and safety, then a concrete agreement should be reached to bring the Mahendranagar air entry point into immediate implementation, even if it requires showing flexibility.

What kind of strategy do you think the Government of Nepal should adopt to bring these issues to a conclusion in the Prime Minister's visit to India and upcoming diplomatic and technical negotiations?

The Government of Nepal should not limit these aviation sector issues to mere formal agendas but should pursue result-oriented diplomatic initiatives. Firstly, a detailed technical study of India's proposed Bagdogra route should be immediately conducted by the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal and a team of aviation experts. If it does not have any significant impact on Nepal's air traffic and safety, then a concrete agreement should be reached to bring the Mahendranagar air entry point into immediate implementation, even if it requires showing flexibility. The commitment made 12 years ago must now be seen in practice, not just in documents and speeches.

Furthermore, to remove the inequality in air connectivity between Nepal and India, diplomatic pressure and dialogue should be intensified to immediately grant written flight permits to Nepali private airline companies like Buddha Air, Shree Airlines, etc., to fly to Delhi and other Indian cities. And along with external diplomatic efforts, internal plans for decentralization of necessary labor, immigration, and tourism-related services and effective marketing to operate the Bhairahawa and Pokhara airports at full capacity should also be implemented simultaneously.
